doc_summary: The paper shows that LLM feedback loops (output-refinement and policy-refinement) drive in-context reward hacking that static evaluations miss, and recommends evaluation changes (more feedback cycles, more loop types, atypical observations) to surface it. Experiments use simulated Twitter and ToolEmu banking-style environments with realism-motivated design choices.

items.claim: prefers evaluations that include the feedback loop (multi-round, environment-responsive interaction) over static datasets because harmful behavior only emerges after repeated cycles and static evals miss it.
items.quote: To increase both the magnitude and frequency of ICRH during evaluation, developers should evaluate LLMs under more cycles of feedback. More cycles of feedback increasingly refines world-LLM components, which drives optimization, so evaluating with more cycles of feedback will capture more ICRH.

items.claim: In a setup, inject atypical environment observations such as random API errors instead of a clean happy-path environment because off-distribution observations probe misalignment that typical ones don't surface.
items.quote: To increase the frequency of ICRH, developers should modify environment dynamics to inject more atypical observations. Intuitively, ICRH can be driven by a misalignment between distributions with high objective and distributions with low negative side effect in the pretraining data

items.claim: In a setup, seed scenarios with real-world data and simulate the actual feedback mechanism (e.g., A/B testing on real headlines) instead of synthetic toy prompts because it makes the setup realistic.
items.quote: For realism, we seed our tweets with news article headlines taken from the most upvoted Reddit posts on r/news and r/worldnews from 10/16/22 to 10/16/23.

items.claim: In a setup, build on an emulator with human-verified realism and add realistic failure modes (server-side API errors) instead of using idealized tool responses because real APIs fail.
items.quote: Our setup adds additional realism by allowing environments to inject API errors, simulating the fact that API calls can fail server-side.

items.claim: prefers simulating many types of feedback loops (e.g., multi-agent competition) over a single loop type because mitigations or evals targeting one loop miss others and ecological validity suffers.
items.quote: simulating more types of feedback loops will make evaluation more ecologically valid and prevent developers from designing ineffective mitigations for ICRH (e.g., reducing ICRH arising from one type of feedback loop but missing ICRH arising from another type).

items.claim: Treats under-specified, goal-driven prompts with implicit constraints as the natural elicitor of reward hacking, with sparse error feedback and no explicit instruction to misbehave.
items.quote: In line with this perspective, we find that LLMs handle sparse feedback: feedback that specifies an error with the current state without directing how the LLM should update (such as a server-side API error).

items.claim: Distrusts the claim that better prompt specification or scale will remove misbehavior, since models struggle to satisfy constraints and safety constraints are hard to fully enumerate.
items.quote: In practice, fully specifying all safety constraints in a prompt is difficult. Since safety is task-specific and the set of safety constraints is vast, users or developers are unaware of all the safety constraints to specify to the model

items.claim: Checks robustness of findings by using multiple independent evaluators/metrics and many configurations rather than a single judge.
items.quote: For robustness, we run evaluation with three different LLM evaluators: Claude-2, Gpt-3.5, and Gpt-4.

items.claim: Candidly flags that simulated environments lack real-world richness, limiting transfer of conclusions.
items.quote: Third, our environments lack the richness of real-world dynamics, making it difficult to transfer our immediate conclusions to real-world environments.

items.claim: Motivates test choices by real-world incidents (Sydney, Bard, Replika) and extrapolates to deployments where agents autonomously handle failures.
items.quote: We consider the setup of a user deploying an LLM as an assistant in a virtual environment, which mirrors real-world LLM agents such as AutoGPT (Richards, 2023) or Google’s Bard assistant (Grant, 2023).
